verified_facts.fact: The core tool is a legal search index. OpenAI states what it covers and how large it is: U.S. case law, statutes, regulations, court rules and administrative decisions across a corpus of more than 230 million URLs, with sources added daily.

verified_facts.verbatim_quote: At the highest reasoning effort for both systems, Astra for Law passed the evaluation’s overall correctness check on 54.0% of questions, compared with 38.7% for GPT‑6 Astra using web search alone – a 40% relative improvement.

But OpenAI never says which COUNTRIES' law firms may join Trusted Access. As checked on both announcement pages to 2026-09-18, no country list for eligibility appears. No price. Nothing on any of the three pages states what Astra for Law costs, whether it is included in an existing ChatGPT Enterprise contract, or what the plugins cost.
No eligibility criteria for Trusted Access: no firm size, no application route, no waitlist, no deadline, no participant count. 'Eligible firms' and 'selected law firms' are used without definition.

No end date, no completion date, and no statement that Astra for Law will ever become generally available.
No statement about Traditional Chinese, Chinese-language legal work, or any non-English drafting. The page names no language at all.

No detail on what Zero Data Retention or exclusion from human review means in practice, or on whether either applies outside the eligible-firm offering.

No statement that ChatGPT for Word's general availability is limited to law firms - OpenAI announces it in the legal post but describes it as generally available. Which plans and regions it covers is NOT stated on this page.

editorial_brief:
READER AND ANGLE. Written for a Taiwanese general reader who is not a lawyer and will never touch this product, but who keeps hearing that AI is about to replace professionals. The question the article answers is: when a frontier lab builds a version of its model for one profession, what does it actually add, and what does that tell you about what the general model could not do? The answer here is unusually concrete and unusually humbling - OpenAI did not train a new model. It added a searchable corpus of one country's law, wrote instructions for legal analysis, put two data-handling terms around it, and restricted it to selected firms. The lesson for a general reader is that the hard part was sources and access rules, not intelligence.

THE CENTRAL FACT TO GET RIGHT. Two scopes that look alike and are not. The search index is explicitly U.S. law. The product's availability geography is NOT STATED AT ALL - OpenAI says 'selected law firms' through 'Trusted Access', with no country list. Writing 'a U.S.-only product' would be an inference from the corpus; writing 'available worldwide' would be an inference from silence. Both are wrong. The second thing to get right is that Cooley's GO Public runs on ChatGPT Work, per OpenAI's own customer story, even though Cooley appears in the Astra for Law announcement.

THE DETAIL THAT EARNS THE PIECE ITS PLACE. 230 million URLs, sources added daily, and a nonprofit's case-law collection are the product. So is the sentence 'reliable authorities the lawyer can examine for herself'. The value proposition is not that the model knows more law; it is that the answer comes with something a professional can go and check. That reframes the whole story for a reader who has ever been given a confident answer with a fake citation.

SUGGESTED FIVE SECTIONS. (1) What was announced on 2026-09-17 and why 'configured' is not 'new model'. (2) What was actually added - the index and its stated jurisdiction, the instructions, and why a checkable citation is the point - ending with the required table (max 4 columns: 項目 / 內容 / 開放對象 / 官方未說明的部分; 4-6 rows covering the model, the index, Trusted Access, ZDR, the plugins, ChatGPT for Word; caption dated 2026-09-18). (3) How to read the benchmark: 200 questions, private validation set, matched reasoning effort, OpenAI's own test - and what 'private validation set' means for anyone who wants to check; diagram goes here. (4) Access and data terms: selected firms, coming soon to the API, ZDR and exclusion from human review scoped to eligible firms, governance being designed with one firm rather than published. (5) What OpenAI did not say, plus the one item in this announcement a general reader can actually use - ChatGPT for Word going generally available, with the plain note that OpenAI stated no plan, region or language for it.

ORIGINAL SCENARIO, to be labelled as an editorial example per BRIEF. A reader asks a general assistant about a contract clause and gets a fluent answer citing a statute number that does not exist. The editorial point is that the fix a professional product reaches for is not a smarter model but a bounded, named, checkable source - and that a reader can apply the same test to any AI answer they are given: can I open what it cited?

TONE AND SCOPE. Plain, no awe, no threat narrative about lawyers' jobs - OpenAI makes no such claim and neither should the article. Deliberately out of scope: any legal advice; any suggestion a reader use AI for their own legal matter; what GPT-6 Astra is (covered 2026-09-03); the general 'industry version of ChatGPT' explainer (covered 2026-09-10); any comparison with Harvey, Legora, Thomson Reuters or any competitor product; any hands-on impression.
